cards.name: Atrioventricular (AV) node
cards.core: The slow gate between atria and ventricles: it delays every impulse by about 0.1 s so the atria finish filling the ventricles, and it filters fast atrial rhythms.

quick.text: Apex of **Koch's triangle**, on the central fibrous body
**Delays** each beat ~0.1 s and **filters** fast atrial rhythms
**Ca²⁺-driven**, poorly coupled cells → slow, decremental conduction
**Inferior MI** → nodal block: narrow escape, atropine works
Lives in the **PR interval**; Wenckebach = nodal block

parts.name: Compact node
parts.note: At the apex of Koch's triangle, on the right-atrial side of the central fibrous body. It continues as the penetrating His bundle.

parts.name: Fast pathway
parts.note: Enters from the upper atrial septum. Conducts quickly but recovers slowly (long refractory period).

parts.name: Slow pathway
parts.note: The inferior nodal extension, running between the coronary-sinus ostium and the tricuspid annulus. Conducts slowly but recovers quickly; the AVNRT ablation target.

anatomy.summary: Compact node at the apex of Koch's triangle, fed by a fast and a slow pathway, continuing as the His bundle.
anatomy.detail: The compact node lies in the floor of the right atrium at the apex of Koch's triangle (tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet hinge, coronary-sinus ostium). It rests on the central fibrous body, just below the membranous septum, and becomes the His bundle where it pierces that fibrous body. Two atrial inputs feed it: a fast pathway from the upper septum and a slow pathway from the region near the coronary-sinus ostium.

function.summary: Slow, Ca²⁺-dependent, decremental conduction: it delays and filters every impulse.
function.detail: Nodal cells depolarise with an L-type Ca²⁺ current instead of a fast Na⁺ current and have few gap junctions (Cx45), so conduction is very slow. The delay accounts for most of the PR interval. Conduction is decremental: the earlier an impulse arrives, the more slowly it passes or the more likely it is blocked, which protects the ventricles in AF and flutter. Vagal tone slows it; sympathetic tone speeds it. If the sinus node fails, junctional cells take over at 40–60/min with a narrow QRS.

supply.summary: AV nodal artery from the dominant artery, usually the RCA.
supply.detail: AV nodal artery, a branch from the dominant artery at the crux of the heart: the RCA in about 80–90% of people, the LCx in left-dominant hearts.

relations.why: Inferior MI often slows or blocks the node: ischaemia of the AV nodal artery plus a strong vagal reflex.

relations.with: Membranous septum and the non-/right coronary aortic cusps
relations.why: The node and His bundle sit just below them, so aortic valve surgery or TAVI can cause heart block.
Tricuspid surgery and VSD closure work right next to the conduction axis.
The slow pathway runs between it and the tricuspid annulus: the target of AVNRT ablation.

echo.text: Not visible itself; it lies at the crux, where the atrial septum meets the tricuspid and mitral hinges.

cut.text: Apex of Koch's triangle, above the coronary-sinus ostium.
At the crux, under the AV valve hinges.

ecg.text: PR interval (best in II): most of it is AV-nodal delay.

complications.name: First-degree AV block
complications.mechanism: Slower nodal conduction from vagal tone, drugs (beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin) or ageing.
complications.presentation: PR > 200 ms, constant; every P is followed by a QRS. Usually no symptoms.

complications.name: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
complications.mechanism: Decremental conduction: each impulse arrives earlier in the node's recovery and passes more slowly, until one fails.
complications.presentation: PR lengthens beat by beat, then a P is not conducted; grouped beating. Usually benign and nodal.
complications.hook: PR grows, then a dropped beat

complications.name: Complete heart block with junctional escape
complications.mechanism: Block within the node (inferior MI, drug toxicity, hyperkalaemia); the junction below takes over.
complications.presentation: P waves and QRS complexes unrelated; narrow escape at 40–60/min. Often responds to atropine.
complications.hook: P and QRS unrelated; narrow escape 40–60/min

complications.name: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
complications.mechanism: A premature beat blocks in the fast pathway (still refractory), goes down the slow pathway and returns up the fast one: a circuit inside the AV junction.
complications.presentation: Sudden regular narrow-complex tachycardia, often 150–250/min; P hidden in the QRS or a pseudo-r′ in V1. Stops with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine.
complications.hook: Regular narrow tachycardia; pseudo-r′ in V1

complications.name: AV block after valve surgery or TAVI
complications.mechanism: The compact node and penetrating His bundle lie just below the aortic root and next to the septal tricuspid hinge; oedema, haematoma or the prosthesis presses on them.
complications.presentation: New PR prolongation, LBBB or complete heart block in the days after the procedure; some patients need a pacemaker.
complications.hook: New LBBB or heart block after aortic procedures

student.text: Its upstroke is carried by Ca²⁺ (not Na⁺) and its cells are poorly coupled. That is also why Ca²⁺-channel blockers and beta-blockers slow it and lidocaine does not.
It lets atrial contraction finish filling the ventricles before they contract.

Wenckebach (PR grows, then a drop) points to the node; Mobitz II (fixed PR, sudden drop) points below it to the His–Purkinje system. Nodal tissue fatigues gradually; His–Purkinje tissue conducts all or nothing.

student.hook: Drugs that act on the node
student.text: Adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem and digoxin all act on the node, which is why they slow the ventricular rate in AF and why adenosine stops re-entry that uses the node (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT).

resident.hook: AV block in inferior STEMI is usually nodal
resident.text: Narrow escape, often transient and atropine-responsive. AV block in anterior STEMI is infranodal: wide escape, worse prognosis, plan for pacing.
Look for reversible causes before pacing (AV-nodal drugs, hyperkalaemia, ischaemia, and Lyme carditis in the right setting).
Adenosine that stops it suggests a node-dependent re-entry (AVNRT/AVRT); adenosine that only slows it and shows flutter waves means the node is a bystander. Record a rhythm strip while giving it.
Never give AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF (irregular, wide, bizarre QRS): blocking the node pushes conduction down the accessory pathway.

fellow.text: Slow-pathway ablation is done in the inferior (posteroseptal) part of Koch's triangle near the CS ostium, away from the compact node at the apex; the main risk is complete heart block.
When pacing is needed, conduction system pacing (His bundle or left bundle branch area) keeps ventricular activation more physiological than RV apical pacing.

saq.q: Why does the AV node conduct slowly?
saq.a: Its cells depolarise with an L-type Ca²⁺ current instead of fast Na⁺ channels and are poorly coupled (few gap junctions), so impulses pass slowly. This delay is most of the PR interval.
keys: Makes most of the PR interval

saq.q: Which type of second-degree AV block points to the AV node, and why?
saq.a: Mobitz I (Wenckebach): the PR lengthens before a dropped beat because nodal tissue fatigues gradually (decremental conduction). A fixed PR with sudden drops (Mobitz II) points below the node.

saq.q: Inferior STEMI with complete heart block and a narrow escape at 45/min. Where is the block, why, and what course do you expect?
saq.a: In the AV node: ischaemia of the AV nodal artery (from the RCA) plus vagal tone. The narrow escape is junctional; the block is often transient and atropine-responsive. Pace only if unstable or persistent.

sources: ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 bradycardia and conduction delay guideline
verify: AV nodal artery from the RCA in about 80–90%

cards.name: Mitral valve
cards.core: The LV inflow valve: two leaflets held by chordae and papillary muscles, closing against the highest pressure in the heart.

quick.text: Between **LA and LV**; the anterior leaflet is the back wall of the **LVOT**
Seals in systole only if **leaflets + chordae + papillary muscles + LV** all work
**PMPM rupture** after inferior MI → acute MR, flash pulmonary oedema
**MR = systolic** murmur; **MS = diastolic** rumble + opening snap
**PLAX** for prolapse; **PSAX** fish-mouth to measure MS

parts.name: Anterior leaflet
parts.note: The larger, deeper leaflet (A1–A3), about one third of the ring. It is in fibrous continuity with the aortic valve (aorto-mitral curtain) and forms one wall of the LV outflow tract.

parts.name: Posterior leaflet
parts.note: Shorter but runs along about two thirds of the ring, with three scallops: P1 (anterolateral), P2 (middle), P3 (posteromedial). P2 is the commonest site of prolapse or flail.

parts.name: Commissures
parts.note: Anterolateral and posteromedial, where the two leaflets meet. Rheumatic disease fuses them first.

anatomy.summary: Two leaflets on a saddle-shaped ring: a large anterior leaflet next to the aortic valve and a scalloped posterior leaflet (P1–P3).
anatomy.detail: Between the left atrium and left ventricle, on a saddle-shaped fibrous ring. The anterior leaflet hangs from the aortic side of the ring; the posterior leaflet from the free (mural) side, next to the left AV groove that holds the circumflex artery and coronary sinus. Chordae from both papillary muscles reach both leaflets: the anterolateral muscle holds the anterolateral half of each leaflet, the posteromedial muscle the other half.

function.summary: Opens for filling (E then A wave) and closes at S1; a tight seal needs the whole apparatus.
function.detail: Opens in diastole: early passive filling (E wave), then the atrial kick (A wave). Closes at the start of systole when LV pressure exceeds LA pressure, making the mitral part of S1. A tight seal needs the whole apparatus working: ring, leaflets, chordae, papillary muscles and the LV wall under them.

supply.summary: Leaflets have almost no vessels; the papillary muscles matter: ALPM two arteries, PMPM one (PDA).
supply.detail: The leaflets have almost no vessels of their own. What matters is the papillary muscles: the anterolateral has a dual supply (LAD diagonals and LCx marginals); the posteromedial usually depends on one artery, the PDA (most often from the RCA).

relations.why: The anterior leaflet forms one wall of the LVOT: systolic anterior motion in HOCM, and spread of endocarditis between the two valves.

relations.with: Circumflex artery and coronary sinus in the left AV groove
relations.why: Both run close to the posterior ring and can be injured during mitral surgery.
Stenosis or regurgitation raises LA pressure, enlarges the LA and leads to AF.

echo.text: Anterior and posterior leaflets opening towards the septum and closing in a line; prolapse is judged here.
The 'fish-mouth' en face: both leaflets and the commissures; planimetry of the stenotic orifice.
Leaflet motion and colour Doppler of inflow and regurgitant jets.

cut.text: From above, with the atria removed: the two leaflets and the ring.
Chordae and both papillary muscles.
Valve between LA and LV, opening and closing with the beat.

ecg.text: No direct sign. Mitral disease enlarges the LA: broad, notched P in II, deep terminal negative P in V1, and often AF.

complications.name: Mitral stenosis (rheumatic)
complications.mechanism: Rheumatic inflammation fuses the commissures and thickens the leaflets, so the opening shrinks and the LA has to push blood through at high pressure.
complications.presentation: Breathlessness that worsens with tachycardia, AF, LA thrombus and stroke; opening snap and low diastolic rumble at the apex.
complications.hook: Rumble + opening snap, AF, LA clot

complications.name: Mitral valve prolapse and flail leaflet
complications.mechanism: Myxomatous, redundant leaflets (most often P2) billow into the LA in systole; a torn chord lets the edge flail.
complications.presentation: Mid-systolic click and late-systolic murmur; a flail gives severe, eccentric regurgitation.
complications.hook: Mid-systolic click; P2 prolapse or flail

complications.name: Acute MR from papillary muscle rupture
complications.mechanism: Infarction of the single-supply posteromedial muscle (inferior MI) lets its chordae tear free.
complications.presentation: Usually 2–7 days after MI: sudden pulmonary oedema and shock; the murmur can be soft or absent because LA and LV pressures equalise quickly.
complications.hook: 2–7 days after inferior MI: sudden oedema, shock

complications.name: Secondary (functional) MR
complications.mechanism: The leaflets are normal, but a dilated or scarred LV pulls the papillary muscles apart (tethering) and widens the ring.
complications.presentation: MR in heart failure or after MI; it improves when the LV is treated.

complications.name: Systolic anterior motion in HOCM
complications.mechanism: Fast flow past the thick septum drags the anterior leaflet into the LVOT.
complications.presentation: Dynamic outflow obstruction plus MR; the murmur gets louder on standing or Valsalva.
complications.hook: Murmur louder on Valsalva or standing

student.text: MR is systolic because the LV pushes back into the LA; MS is diastolic because the LA has to push forward into the LV.
In acute MR a small, stiff LA turns the leak into high LA pressure and pulmonary oedema; in chronic MR a big, compliant LA absorbs it for years.
The posteromedial papillary muscle ruptures, not the anterolateral one, because it usually has only one artery (the PDA).
A shorter diastole leaves less time to fill across the narrow valve, so LA pressure jumps (exercise, AF, pregnancy).

resident.text: An LVEF of 60% is already borderline. Refer for intervention when symptomatic, or when asymptomatic with LVEF ≤ 60% or LVESD ≥ 40 mm.
Anticoagulate with a vitamin K antagonist, not a DOAC (INVICTUS).
New murmur or sudden pulmonary oedema a few days after inferior MI: urgent echo for papillary muscle rupture (or VSD); this is surgical.

resident.hook: Secondary MR: treat the LV first
resident.text: In secondary MR, start by treating the LV (guideline-directed medical therapy, CRT if indicated) before judging how severe the MR really is.

fellow.text: Repair beats replacement when durable repair is likely. Secondary MR: transcatheter edge-to-edge repair helps selected patients on optimal medical therapy (COAPT vs MITRA-FR, proportionate vs disproportionate MR).

saq.q: Why does acute MR cause pulmonary oedema when chronic MR of the same size may be tolerated for years?
saq.a: In acute MR the LA is small and stiff, so the leak raises LA and pulmonary venous pressure sharply. In chronic MR the LA enlarges and becomes compliant, absorbing the volume at lower pressure.

saq.q: Why does a fast heart rate make mitral stenosis worse?
saq.a: A shorter diastole leaves less time for blood to cross the narrow valve, so LA pressure rises and the lungs congest.
keys: Less filling time across the valve

saq.q: Asymptomatic severe primary MR, LVEF 58%, LVESD 42 mm. Does she need intervention?
saq.a: Yes: severe primary MR with LVEF ≤ 60% or LVESD ≥ 40 mm is an indication for mitral surgery even without symptoms; repair is preferred.

sources: ASE recommendations on native valve regurgitation (2017)

cards.name: Left anterior descending artery (LAD)
cards.core: The artery of the front of the heart: it feeds the anterior LV wall, most of the septum and the apex, the largest share of LV muscle.

quick.text: Runs down the **anterior interventricular groove** to the apex
Feeds the **anterior wall, apex, front ⅔ of the septum** (+ RBB, LAF)
Occlusion → **ST elevation V1–V4** (+ I, aVL if proximal)
**Wellens** T waves = critical proximal stenosis: angiogram, no stress test
New **RBBB** in anterior MI = big septal infarct, heart-block risk

parts.name: Proximal LAD
parts.note: From the left main to the first septal or first diagonal branch. Occlusion here is the 'widow-maker': the whole territory is at risk.

parts.name: Mid and distal LAD
parts.note: Down the anterior groove to the apex; often wraps round the apex onto the inferior wall.

parts.name: Septal perforators
parts.note: Dive into the front two thirds of the septum and feed the right bundle branch and left anterior fascicle.

anatomy.summary: From the left main down the front groove to the apex, giving septal and diagonal branches.
anatomy.detail: Arises from the left main coronary artery behind the pulmonary trunk and runs down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex, often wrapping round it. Its branches are the septal perforators (into the septum) and the diagonals (over the anterolateral wall). The great cardiac vein runs beside it.

function.summary: Supplies the largest share of LV muscle and two conduction fascicles; flow is mainly in diastole.
function.detail: Supplies the anterior wall, the anterior two thirds of the septum and the apex, and part of the anterolateral papillary muscle (via the diagonals). Through the septal branches it feeds the right bundle branch and the left anterior fascicle. Like all LV coronary flow, most of its flow happens in diastole, when the muscle relaxes.

supply.summary: Territory: anterior and anteroseptal LV and apex; drains through the great cardiac vein.
supply.detail: Territory: anterior and anteroseptal LV, apex, anterior two thirds of the septum; the right bundle branch and left anterior fascicle. Drainage: great cardiac vein to the coronary sinus.

relations.why: An LAD occlusion can cause new RBBB or bifascicular block, a sign of a large infarct and a risk of complete heart block.
Runs alongside in the same groove.
The preferred bypass graft to the LAD.

echo.text: Anteroseptal wall (upper wall in this view).
Anterior and anteroseptal segments at mid-ventricle.
Apical segments and the apex.

cut.text: Anterior and anteroseptal LV wall.

ecg.text: V1–V2 (septum) and V3–V4 (anterior wall); I and aVL too when a proximal occlusion includes the first diagonal.

complications.name: Anterior STEMI
complications.mechanism: Plaque rupture and thrombus in the LAD; the larger the territory beyond the clot, the bigger the infarct.
complications.presentation: ST elevation in V1–V4 (± I, aVL); a large anterior MI lowers the EF and leads to heart failure.
complications.hook: ST↑ V1–V4; largest infarct, heart-failure risk

complications.name: Critical proximal stenosis (Wellens pattern)
complications.mechanism: A tight proximal LAD lesion that has briefly occluded and reopened.
complications.presentation: Pain-free ECG with deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3, normal or slightly raised troponin; high risk of a large anterior MI.
complications.hook: Pain-free, deep or biphasic T in V2–V3

complications.name: New RBBB or bifascicular block
complications.mechanism: Infarction of the septum where the septal perforators feed the right bundle and left anterior fascicle.
complications.presentation: Wide QRS with RBBB ± left axis deviation in an anterior MI; risk of sudden complete heart block.
complications.hook: Wide QRS in anterior MI → pacing risk

complications.name: LV apical aneurysm and thrombus
complications.mechanism: The dead apical wall thins and bulges; blood stagnates there.
complications.presentation: Persistent ST elevation weeks after MI; LV thrombus on echo; risk of stroke.

complications.name: Ventricular septal rupture
complications.mechanism: Necrosis of the apical septum tears, making a left-to-right shunt.
complications.presentation: Days after MI: new harsh holosystolic murmur, shock, step-up in oxygen saturation in the RV.
complications.hook: Days later: new harsh murmur, shock

student.hook: Map the leads to the walls
student.text: V1–V2 septum, V3–V4 anterior wall, I and aVL high lateral (first diagonal). ST elevation from V1 to V4 means an LAD territory.
Coronary flow to the LV happens mainly in diastole. Tachycardia shortens diastole, so it cuts supply just as demand rises.

student.hook: Why anterior MI is the worst
student.text: The LAD feeds the most LV muscle, which is why anterior MI carries the highest risk of heart failure and shock.
The septal branches feed the right bundle and left anterior fascicle, so a new RBBB in anterior MI means a big septal infarct.

resident.text: Chest pain earlier, now pain-free, deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 = critical proximal LAD stenosis. Arrange angiography; do not do a stress test.
de Winter pattern (upsloping ST depression with tall, symmetrical T waves in V1–V6) is a STEMI equivalent of LAD occlusion: activate the cath lab.
After a large anterior MI, look for LV thrombus at the apex on echo before discharge; contrast echo or CMR finds more than plain echo.

fellow.text: A 'wrap-around' LAD can make an anterior occlusion also raise ST in the inferior leads.
The long patency of a LIMA-to-LAD graft is a key reason bypass surgery can outperform PCI in complex multivessel disease, especially with diabetes.

saq.q: ST elevation in V1–V4: which artery, and which other leads suggest the block is proximal?
saq.a: The LAD. ST elevation also in I and aVL (first diagonal territory) suggests a proximal occlusion.

saq.q: Why does a new RBBB in anterior MI suggest a large infarct?
saq.a: The right bundle (and left anterior fascicle) are fed by the LAD's septal branches. New block means the septum is infarcted: a large territory with a risk of complete heart block.

saq.q: Pain-free after chest pain; deep, symmetrical T inversion in V2–V3; troponin normal. Diagnosis and next test?
saq.a: Wellens pattern: critical proximal LAD stenosis. Arrange coronary angiography and avoid stress testing.

cards.name: Right atrium
cards.core: The receiving chamber for the body's venous blood and the home of the heart's pacemaker.

quick.text: Receives the **SVC, IVC and coronary sinus**; right heart border on CXR
**JVP** = RA pressure gauge: no valve in between
Makes the **first half of the P**; tall P in II = RA enlargement
**Typical flutter** circles the tricuspid ring through the **CTI**
**IVC** size and collapse estimate RA pressure

anatomy.summary: Smooth back (sinus venarum) and ridged front (pectinate muscles) meet at the crista terminalis.
anatomy.detail: Receives the SVC (top), the IVC (floor) and the coronary sinus (between the IVC opening and the tricuspid valve), and empties through the tricuspid valve into the RV. Its smooth back part (sinus venarum) and its rough front part with pectinate muscles, which run on into the right atrial appendage, meet at the crista terminalis. Its septal wall holds the fossa ovalis; its floor holds Koch's triangle and the cavotricuspid isthmus. It forms the right heart border on a frontal chest X-ray.

function.summary: Reservoir, conduit and booster pump at low pressure; the JVP shows its waves.
function.detail: Works in three phases: a reservoir while the ventricles contract, a conduit in early diastole and a booster pump (atrial kick) at the end of diastole. Pressure is low, normally about 2–6 mmHg. With no valve between it and the internal jugular vein, the JVP shows its pressure and waves (a, c, v).

supply.summary: RCA atrial branches; the SA nodal artery (RCA in ~60%).
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the RCA. The SA nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 60% of people and from the LCx in about 40%.

relations.why: The SA node lies here; a sinus venosus ASD sits at the same junction.
The typical flutter circuit runs around the tricuspid ring and through the isthmus.
Its thin wall collapses early when fluid compresses the heart (tamponade).

echo.text: Bottom chamber on the screen's left (apex at the top); RA area.
Close to the probe; RA collapse in tamponade.
The IVC entering the RA; its size and collapse estimate RA pressure.

cut.text: Opened from the side: crista, pectinate muscles, fossa ovalis, Koch's triangle.
Upper chamber on the patient's right.

ecg.text: First part of the P wave. RA enlargement: tall, peaked P in II (> 2.5 mm).

complications.name: Typical atrial flutter
complications.mechanism: A large re-entry circuit around the tricuspid ring, through the slow cavotricuspid isthmus.
complications.presentation: Saw-tooth flutter waves in II, III and aVF, often 2:1 block with a ventricular rate near 150/min.
complications.hook: Saw-tooth in II, III, aVF; rate ~150 (2:1)

complications.name: Right atrial enlargement
complications.mechanism: Chronic pressure or volume load: tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension, ASD.
complications.presentation: Tall P waves, atrial arrhythmias, raised JVP.

complications.name: RA collapse in tamponade
complications.mechanism: Pericardial pressure exceeds the low RA pressure, so the wall buckles inwards.
complications.presentation: Hypotension, raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus; on echo the RA wall folds in during systole.
complications.hook: RA wall folds in during systole

student.text: The JVP is a pressure gauge on the RA: no valve stands between the internal jugular vein and the atrium.

student.hook: The RA makes the first half of P
student.text: The RA fires first, so it makes the first half of the P wave; a tall, peaked P in II means RA enlargement.
The smooth part comes from the embryonic sinus venosus, the ridged part from the primitive atrium; the crista terminalis is the seam.

resident.hook: Estimate RA pressure from the IVC
resident.text: ≤ 2.1 cm and collapsing > 50% on a sniff ≈ 3 mmHg; > 2.1 cm and collapsing < 50% ≈ 15 mmHg.
In tamponade, RA collapse lasting more than a third of the cycle is sensitive; RV diastolic collapse is more specific.
Kussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration) points to constriction, restriction or severe RV failure.

saq.q: Why can the JVP be used to estimate right atrial pressure?
saq.a: There is no valve between the internal jugular vein and the RA, so the height of the venous column reflects RA pressure.
keys: No valve between IJV and RA

saq.q: Describe the circuit of typical atrial flutter and its ECG.
saq.a: A large re-entry circuit around the tricuspid ring through the cavotricuspid isthmus. Saw-tooth flutter waves in II, III and aVF; atrial rate ~300/min, often 2:1 block giving ~150/min.

saq.q: IVC 2.4 cm, collapsing less than 50% on a sniff. Estimate RA pressure and say what it means.
saq.a: About 15 mmHg: raised RA pressure, e.g. RV failure, tamponade or fluid overload.

cards.name: Right ventricle
cards.core: A thin-walled, crescent-shaped pump that pushes blood through the low-pressure lungs, and fails quickly when that pressure rises suddenly.

quick.text: Most **anterior** chamber, behind the sternum; a crescent round the LV
Low-pressure **volume pump** that contracts lengthways (TAPSE)
**PE**: the dilated RV pushes the septum → D-shaped LV, shock
**RV infarct** (proximal RCA): hypotension, clear lungs, **no nitrates**
Recognise it by the **moderator band** and the more apical tricuspid hinge

anatomy.summary: Inlet, trabeculated apex with the moderator band, and a smooth outlet (RVOT).
anatomy.detail: The most anterior chamber, right behind the sternum. It wraps around the LV: triangular in the 4-chamber view, a crescent in short axis. Three parts: an inlet (tricuspid valve, chordae, papillary muscles), a coarsely trabeculated apex crossed by the moderator band, and a smooth outlet (infundibulum, RVOT) to the pulmonary valve. A muscular ridge (supraventricular crest) separates the tricuspid and pulmonary valves. The free wall is thin, normally under 5 mm.

function.summary: A thin volume pump that shares the septum with the LV (interdependence).
function.detail: A volume pump into a low-resistance circuit: systolic pressure about 15–30 mmHg. It contracts mainly lengthways, pulling the tricuspid ring towards the apex. It shares the septum with the LV, so each ventricle's pressure and volume change the other's shape and filling (ventricular interdependence).

supply.summary: Mostly RCA; the front from the LAD, the inferior part from the PDA.
supply.detail: Mostly the RCA (RV branches, acute marginal, conus branch); the anterior part from the LAD; the inferior part from the PDA. Because RV pressure is low, it is perfused in systole as well as diastole.

relations.why: The chamber most often hit by penetrating chest wounds and the closest to the probe in subcostal views.
An overloaded RV flattens the septum and squeezes the LV (D-shaped LV).
Carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.

echo.text: Triangular chamber; RV basal diameter vs LV; TAPSE.
Crescent around the LV; a D-shaped LV means RV overload.
RV free wall thickness and diastolic collapse in tamponade.
RVOT at the top of the image.

cut.text: Opened: trabeculae, moderator band, tricuspid valve, RVOT.
Triangular chamber; tricuspid hinge more apical than the mitral.
Crescent wrapped round the LV.

ecg.text: V1–V2 and right-sided leads (V4R). RV hypertrophy: right axis, dominant R in V1. RV infarction: ST elevation in V4R.

complications.name: Acute RV failure in pulmonary embolism
complications.mechanism: A thin RV meets a sudden rise in pulmonary pressure, dilates and pushes the septum into the LV, so the LV underfills and output falls.
complications.presentation: Breathlessness, tachycardia, hypotension; ECG sinus tachycardia, new RBBB, T inversion V1–V4, S1Q3T3; echo RV dilated, free wall hypokinetic with the apex spared (McConnell sign).

complications.name: RV infarction
complications.mechanism: Proximal RCA occlusion takes out the RV branches; the RV stops pumping and the LV is starved of preload.
complications.presentation: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs; ST elevation in V4R; very sensitive to nitrates.

complications.name: RV hypertrophy and cor pulmonale
complications.mechanism: Chronic pulmonary hypertension (lung disease, left heart disease, thromboembolic) thickens then dilates the RV.
complications.presentation: Right axis, dominant R in V1, raised JVP, oedema, loud P2.
complications.hook: Right axis, dominant R in V1

complications.name: Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy
complications.mechanism: Desmosome gene defects let fibrofatty tissue replace RV muscle, creating scar for re-entry.
complications.presentation: VT with LBBB pattern, T inversion in V1–V3, epsilon wave; sudden death in young athletes.

student.text: Pulmonary pressures are about a fifth of systemic, so by Laplace's law the wall needs far less thickness to carry the same stroke volume.

student.hook: The RV and LV are in series
student.text: Over a few beats their stroke volumes must match, so a failing RV starves the LV.
How to tell the RV on echo or at surgery: moderator band, coarse trabeculae, tricuspid hinge closer to the apex, and no fibrous link between its inlet and outlet valves.
ST elevation there means the RV is involved.

resident.text: Avoid nitrates and diuretics, give cautious fluids, keep AV synchrony (pace if blocked).
In PE, an RV/LV diameter ratio > 1 on echo or CT marks RV dysfunction and a higher-risk patient.
TAPSE < 17 mm suggests RV systolic dysfunction.

saq.q: Why is the RV wall thinner than the LV wall?
saq.a: The pulmonary circulation runs at low pressure. By Laplace's law, lower pressure needs less wall thickness to keep wall stress normal.
keys: Laplace: wall stress ∝ P × r / thickness

saq.q: In an inferior STEMI, which extra lead looks for RV infarction, and what confirms it?
saq.a: V4R; ST elevation of 1 mm or more.

saq.q: Inferior STEMI; after sublingual nitrate the patient is hypotensive with a raised JVP and clear lungs. Explain and manage.
saq.a: RV infarction: the RV depends on preload and the nitrate dropped it. Stop nitrates, give cautious IV fluid, keep AV synchrony (pace if blocked), reperfuse urgently; inotropes if still low.

cards.name: Left atrium
cards.core: The chamber behind the mitral valve: its pressure is what the lungs feel, and it is where atrial fibrillation starts.

quick.text: Most **posterior** chamber, right in front of the **oesophagus**
Its pressure is what the **lungs feel** (≈ wedge pressure)
**AF** starts at the **pulmonary-vein** sleeves
LA enlargement: **broad notched P** in II, deep negative P in V1
**Myxoma**: commonest primary cardiac tumour, usually here

anatomy.summary: Posterior chamber receiving four pulmonary veins, with the LAA off its front-left side.
anatomy.detail: The most posterior chamber, lying directly in front of the oesophagus and the descending aorta, above the left main bronchus. The four pulmonary veins (two from each side) enter its smooth back wall; the trabeculated left atrial appendage arises from its front-left side. Its septal wall faces the RA across the fossa ovalis; it empties through the mitral valve into the LV.

function.summary: Reservoir, conduit and booster pump; the atrial kick adds about a fifth to a third of filling.
function.detail: Reservoir, conduit and booster pump, like the RA. The atrial kick adds about a fifth to a third of LV filling, more in a stiff ventricle. Without mitral stenosis, LA pressure ≈ pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≈ LV end-diastolic pressure.

supply.summary: LCx atrial branches.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the LCx, and the SA nodal artery when it comes from the LCx.

relations.why: The window for transoesophageal echo; also the reason AF ablation on the back wall can injure the oesophagus.
Muscle sleeves in the veins fire the ectopic beats that start most AF.
A very large LA widens the carina on chest X-ray.

echo.text: Behind the aortic root; LA diameter.
LA volume (with the 2-chamber view).
Below the aortic valve in this view.

cut.text: Opened: pulmonary vein openings, LAA, septum.
Upper chamber on the patient's left.
Above the mitral valve.

ecg.text: Second part of the P wave. LA enlargement: P ≥ 120 ms and notched in II; deep terminal negative P in V1.

complications.name: Atrial fibrillation
complications.mechanism: Pulmonary-vein triggers fire into an atrium that stretch and fibrosis have made able to sustain many wavelets.
complications.presentation: Irregularly irregular narrow-QRS rhythm with no P waves; palpitations, heart failure, stroke.

complications.name: LA enlargement
complications.mechanism: Chronic pressure or volume load: mitral disease, LV diastolic dysfunction, AF itself.
complications.presentation: Broad notched P waves, AF; on echo an LA volume above normal.

complications.name: Pulmonary oedema from raised LA pressure
complications.mechanism: LA pressure passes straight back to the pulmonary capillaries; above about 18–25 mmHg fluid leaks into the lung.
complications.presentation: Breathlessness, orthopnoea, crackles, interstitial then alveolar oedema on X-ray.

complications.name: Left atrial myxoma
complications.mechanism: The commonest primary cardiac tumour, usually on a stalk near the fossa ovalis, swinging into the mitral orifice.
complications.presentation: Positional breathlessness or syncope, 'tumour plop', emboli, fever and weight loss.

student.hook: LA pressure is what the lungs feel
student.text: When it rises, fluid moves into the lung interstitium, then the alveoli. The wedge pressure is a stand-in for it.
The LA fires second, so LA enlargement widens and notches the P wave in II and deepens the negative end of the P in V1.
Losing the atrial kick (in AF) hurts most when the LV is stiff (LVH, aortic stenosis, HCM) or the mitral valve is narrow.
Myxoma is the commonest primary cardiac tumour, and it usually sits in the LA.

resident.hook: LA volume index > 34 mL/m² is enlarged
resident.text: A marker of chronically raised filling pressure and of AF risk.
Before cardioversion of AF lasting 48 h or more without 3 weeks of anticoagulation, TOE excludes LA/LAA thrombus (the oesophagus lies right behind the LA).
Sudden pulmonary oedema with a normal-sized LV and LA: think of an acute valve lesion (papillary muscle or chordal rupture).

saq.q: Why does a rise in LA pressure cause pulmonary oedema?
saq.a: No valves separate the LA from the pulmonary veins, so LA pressure raises pulmonary capillary pressure and pushes fluid into the interstitium, then the alveoli.
keys: No valve between LA and pulmonary veins

saq.q: Where do the triggers of most atrial fibrillation come from?
saq.a: The muscle sleeves of the pulmonary veins where they join the LA.

saq.q: AF started about 5 days ago with no anticoagulation; the patient wants cardioversion now. What do you need first?
saq.a: Exclude LA/LAA thrombus with TOE (or anticoagulate for 3 weeks first), then continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion.

cards.name: Left ventricle
cards.core: The main pump: a thick-walled, bullet-shaped ventricle that drives blood into the high-pressure systemic circulation.

quick.text: High-pressure **pump** that shortens, thickens and twists
**LAD** front + apex · **LCx** lateral · **RCA/PDA** inferior
**Laplace**: pressure load → thick wall; volume load → big chamber
The **subendocardium** is ischaemic first (ST depression)
EF from the **apical views**; wall motion in **PSAX**

anatomy.summary: Thick, conical chamber forming the apex, with two papillary muscles and a smooth LVOT.
anatomy.detail: Posterior and to the left, forming the apex and most of the left heart border. Inlet through the mitral valve, a finely trabeculated apex, two papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial), and a smooth outflow (LVOT) under the aortic valve, which is in fibrous continuity with the mitral valve. The wall is about 0.6–1.0 cm thick. For wall motion it is divided into the AHA 17 segments: 6 basal, 6 mid, 4 apical and the apex.

function.summary: Pressure pump (EF 55–70%); relaxing needs energy (SERCA).
function.detail: A pressure pump reaching about 120 mmHg in systole. Its fibres run in helical layers, so it shortens, thickens and twists. Normal ejection fraction is about 55–70%. Diastole needs energy: Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SERCA) so the muscle relaxes and the ventricle can fill at low pressure.

supply.summary: Three coronaries by wall; the subendocardium is the most vulnerable layer.
supply.detail: LAD: anterior wall, anterior septum, apex. LCx: lateral wall. RCA (PDA): inferior wall and inferior septum (dominance varies). The subendocardium is the most vulnerable layer: highest wall stress, and squeezed during systole.

relations.why: Shared with the RV: RV overload flattens it into a D-shaped LV.
LV dilation or scarring pulls the papillary muscles apart and causes secondary MR.
Each wall segment has a typical artery, so wall-motion patterns localise the culprit.

echo.text: LV diameters and wall thickness.
All walls at mid-ventricle: regional wall motion.
Ejection fraction (biplane method) and apical segments.
LV outflow tract.

cut.text: Opened: papillary muscles, chordae, LVOT.
The long chamber running down to the apex.
Round LV with the crescent RV.

ecg.text: Most of the QRS (I, aVL, V5–V6). LVH: tall voltages (e.g. S in V1 + R in V5/V6 ≥ 35 mm) with strain-type ST–T changes.

complications.name: Myocardial infarction (by wall)
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of the artery feeding a territory; tap the outer LV wall to see which artery and the matching ECG.
complications.presentation: Chest pain, ST changes in the leads facing that wall, regional wall-motion loss on echo.
complications.hook: Tap the outer wall to see its artery

complications.name: Heart failure with reduced EF
complications.mechanism: Lost or weak muscle (infarction, cardiomyopathy) dilates the LV; output falls and filling pressure rises.
complications.presentation: Breathlessness, fatigue, oedema; EF ≤ 40%.

complications.name: LV hypertrophy and HFpEF
complications.mechanism: Pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) thickens the wall; it relaxes poorly, so filling pressure rises.
complications.presentation: Breathlessness with a normal EF, LVH voltages, AF.

complications.name: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
complications.mechanism: Sarcomere gene mutation; asymmetric, often septal, thickening.
complications.presentation: Exertional symptoms, outflow murmur, sudden death risk.

complications.name: Free-wall rupture after MI
complications.mechanism: A thin, necrotic wall tears, usually within the first week.
complications.presentation: Sudden tamponade, electromechanical dissociation, death unless treated surgically at once.
complications.hook: Sudden tamponade within a week of MI

student.text: Laplace's law (wall stress ∝ pressure × radius ÷ wall thickness) explains remodelling: pressure overload thickens the wall (concentric), volume overload dilates the chamber (eccentric).
Highest wall stress and squeezed in systole. Subendocardial ischaemia gives ST depression; transmural injury gives ST elevation.
The LV that cannot squeeze (HFrEF) and the LV that cannot relax (HFpEF). Both raise LA pressure and congest the lungs.
EF = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume; normal is about 55–70%.

resident.text: Reduced ≤ 40%, mildly reduced 41–49%, preserved ≥ 50%.
Wall-motion loss that matches one coronary territory points to ischaemia; loss that crosses territories suggests cardiomyopathy, myocarditis or takotsubo (apical ballooning).
ECG criteria for LVH are specific but insensitive: use echo to measure wall thickness.

fellow.hook: Global longitudinal strain falls before EF does
fellow.text: A relative fall of more than 15% flags early cardiotoxicity in cardio-oncology.

saq.q: Use Laplace's law to explain why aortic stenosis thickens the LV and aortic regurgitation dilates it.
saq.a: Wall stress ∝ pressure × radius ÷ thickness. AS raises pressure, so the wall thickens to normalise stress (concentric). AR adds volume, so the chamber enlarges (eccentric), with some thickening to match.

saq.q: Why is the subendocardium the first layer to become ischaemic?
saq.a: It has the highest wall stress and its vessels are squeezed during systole, so it is perfused only in diastole and runs out of supply first.

saq.q: LVEF 45% with heart failure symptoms. Classify it and name one drug class with strong evidence in this range.
saq.a: Heart failure with mildly reduced EF (41–49%). An SGLT2 inhibitor has strong evidence here.

cards.name: Left atrial appendage
cards.core: A narrow, finger-like pouch off the left atrium: the commonest source of blood clots in atrial fibrillation.

quick.text: Finger-like pouch off the **front-left** of the LA, over the LCx
In **AF** it stops contracting → **stasis → clot → stroke**
Score with **CHA₂DS₂-VA**; DOAC unless MS or a mechanical valve
**TOE** before cardioversion if AF ≥ 48 h without anticoagulation

anatomy.summary: Narrow-necked, ridged, often multilobed pouch beside the left upper pulmonary vein.
anatomy.detail: Arises from the front-left of the LA, between the LA and the pulmonary trunk, lying over the left AV groove with the circumflex artery underneath. A muscular ridge (left lateral ridge) separates its opening from the left upper pulmonary vein. It is lined with pectinate muscles, has a narrow neck and often several lobes; its shape varies (described as chicken wing, windsock, cactus, cauliflower).

function.summary: Compliant reservoir; contracts in sinus rhythm, still in AF.
function.detail: A compliant reservoir that eases LA pressure when volume rises, and a source of natriuretic peptide when stretched. In sinus rhythm it contracts and empties briskly; in AF it barely moves.

supply.summary: LCx atrial branches.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the LCx.

relations.why: Runs just under it; at risk with surgical clips or occlusion devices.
The ridge between them can look like a mass on echo.
Runs over it; at risk during ablation or LAA procedures.

echo.text: Sometimes seen beside the aortic root; TOE shows it far better.

cut.text: Its opening on the front-left wall of the LA.

ecg.text: No sign of its own.

complications.name: Thrombus and embolic stroke in AF
complications.mechanism: No contraction plus a narrow, trabeculated pouch gives stasis (Virchow); most LA clots in non-valvular AF form here.
complications.presentation: Stroke, TIA, limb or bowel ischaemia; thrombus seen on TOE.
complications.hook: Stroke in AF; clot seen on TOE

complications.name: Ridge mistaken for thrombus
complications.mechanism: The left lateral ridge or pectinate muscles can look like a mass.
complications.presentation: Imaging pitfall; avoid treating a normal structure as clot.
complications.hook: A normal ridge that mimics clot

student.text: Stasis (no contraction in AF), a narrow neck and a ridged lining. About 90% of LA thrombi in non-valvular AF are in the appendage.

student.hook: AF stroke risk is scored, not guessed
student.text: The ESC 2024 guideline uses CHA₂DS₂-VA.

resident.text: AF lasting 48 h or more (or unknown) without 3 weeks of anticoagulation: TOE to exclude LAA thrombus before cardioversion, and anticoagulate for at least 4 weeks after.
Choose a DOAC over warfarin, except with moderate–severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve.
LAA occlusion (percutaneous device or surgical) is an option for patients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation.

saq.q: Why does thrombus form in the left atrial appendage in AF?
saq.a: In AF the appendage stops contracting; its narrow neck and ridged lining make blood stagnate (Virchow's stasis), so clot forms there.

saq.q: A 70-year-old man with AF, hypertension and diabetes. Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VA and decide on anticoagulation.
saq.a: Age 65–74 = 1, hypertension = 1, diabetes = 1: score 3. Anticoagulate, preferably with a DOAC.

verify: ~90% of LA thrombi in non-valvular AF in the LAA

cards.name: Left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT)
cards.core: The smooth channel under the aortic valve, between the septum and the anterior mitral leaflet: where outflow obstruction happens.

quick.text: Between the **basal septum** and the **anterior mitral leaflet**
**HCM**: SAM blocks it; worse with **Valsalva, standing, dehydration**
Obstructive HCM: avoid **nitrates and inotropes**; give fluid
Measure it in **PLAX**; Doppler gradient in **A5C**

anatomy.summary: Smooth channel under the aortic valve, with the membranous septum and His bundle at its top.
anatomy.detail: Bounded in front by the basal ventricular septum and behind by the anterior mitral leaflet (the aorto-mitral curtain), it ends at the aortic valve ring. It is smooth, without trabeculae. The membranous septum lies at its top, under the right and non-coronary aortic cusps, with the His bundle just below.

function.summary: Ejection conduit; LVOT area × VTI gives stroke volume.
function.detail: A conduit for ejection. Its cross-section times the velocity–time integral (VTI) of flow through it gives stroke volume by Doppler, and it is the reference point of the continuity equation for aortic stenosis.

supply.summary: Septal side from LAD perforators.
supply.detail: The septal side from LAD septal perforators.

relations.why: Can be pulled into the outflow (systolic anterior motion).
Thickening narrows the channel (HCM, sigmoid septum in older people).
Surgery or devices here can cause heart block.

echo.text: Diameter measured just below the aortic valve in mid-systole; SAM visible here.
Pulsed Doppler for VTI; continuous Doppler for gradients.

cut.text: Between the septum and the anterior mitral leaflet.
Leading up to the aortic valve.

ecg.text: No sign of its own.

complications.name: Dynamic obstruction in HCM
complications.mechanism: A thick basal septum narrows the tract; fast flow drags the anterior mitral leaflet into it (SAM).
complications.presentation: Exertional breathlessness or syncope; murmur louder on standing or Valsalva, softer on squatting.

complications.name: Subaortic membrane
complications.mechanism: A fibrous ridge below the valve makes a fixed narrowing; the jet damages the aortic cusps.
complications.presentation: Outflow murmur, aortic regurgitation; seen on TTE/TOE.

complications.name: Obstruction in hyperdynamic states
complications.mechanism: Low preload plus strong contraction (dehydration, inotropes, takotsubo with a hyperkinetic base) narrows the outflow.
complications.presentation: Hypotension that worsens with inotropes and improves with fluid.

student.text: In HCM, anything that makes the LV smaller or more forceful worsens the obstruction (standing, Valsalva, dehydration, inotropes, vasodilators); anything that fills it eases it (squatting, handgrip, leg raise).
The basis of Doppler cardiac output.

resident.text: Avoid nitrates, vasodilators, aggressive diuresis and inotropes; use beta-blockers or verapamil, give fluid; phenylephrine if hypotensive.
A gradient ≥ 30 mmHg means obstruction; ≥ 50 mmHg with symptoms despite medicines is the threshold for septal reduction.
The LVOT diameter is squared in the continuity equation, so a small measuring error makes a large error in valve area.

fellow.text: Cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten) lower outflow gradients in obstructive HCM; EF has to be monitored.

saq.q: Which manoeuvres make the HCM murmur louder, and why?
saq.a: Standing and Valsalva reduce preload, so the LV gets smaller and the outflow narrows more; squatting and handgrip do the opposite and soften it.
keys: Less preload → smaller LV → more obstruction

saq.q: A patient with obstructive HCM becomes hypotensive after a diuretic. Why, and what do you give?
saq.a: Lower preload worsens the outflow obstruction. Give IV fluid, stop diuretics and vasodilators, use phenylephrine if needed, continue the beta-blocker, and avoid inotropes.

cards.name: Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT)
cards.core: The smooth muscular funnel from the RV to the pulmonary valve, and the commonest source of benign ventricular ectopic beats.

quick.text: Smooth funnel to the **pulmonary valve**, crossing in front of the aortic root
PVC with **LBBB shape + inferior axis** = RVOT origin
Idiopathic RVOT ectopy is **triggered (cAMP)**, so adenosine can stop it
Red flags → think **ARVC** (epsilon wave, T inversion beyond V3)

anatomy.summary: Smooth infundibulum, separated from the RV inlet by the supraventricular crest.
anatomy.detail: The most anterior part of the heart, under the sternum. A smooth-walled funnel (infundibulum) separated from the tricuspid inlet by the supraventricular crest. The pulmonary valve sits on top, higher and to the left of the aortic valve. Behind it lies the aortic root (right and left coronary sinuses), so the two outflow tracts cross.

function.summary: Carries RV output; a short Doppler acceleration time hints at pulmonary hypertension.
function.detail: Carries RV output to the pulmonary valve. Doppler of its flow helps judge pulmonary pressure: a short acceleration time suggests pulmonary hypertension.

supply.summary: Conus branch and LAD branches.
supply.detail: Conus branch (from the RCA or its own ostium) and LAD branches.

relations.with: Aortic root (right and left coronary sinuses)
relations.why: Some 'outflow tract' ectopy comes from the aortic cusps just behind it.
Close by: a risk during ablation in this region.
Narrowing below or at the valve (infundibular or valvar stenosis) loads the RV.

echo.text: Wrapping round the aortic valve to the pulmonary valve.
The chamber at the top of the image.

cut.text: The smooth funnel up to the pulmonary valve.

ecg.text: RVOT ectopy: LBBB-like QRS with an inferior axis (tall R in II, III, aVF) and a transition around V3–V4.

complications.name: Idiopathic outflow-tract PVCs and VT
complications.mechanism: cAMP-driven Ca²⁺ overload causes triggered beats (delayed afterdepolarisations), so stress and exercise bring them on and adenosine can stop them.
complications.presentation: Palpitations; frequent monomorphic PVCs or VT with LBBB-like QRS and inferior axis in a normal heart.
complications.hook: LBBB + inferior axis in a normal heart

complications.name: Tetralogy of Fallot
complications.mechanism: The outlet septum is displaced forwards and narrows the RVOT; with a VSD, blood shunts right to left.
complications.presentation: Cyanosis and 'tet spells' in infancy; repaired adults may have pulmonary regurgitation and VT.

complications.name: RVOT involvement in ARVC
complications.mechanism: Fibrofatty replacement dilates and scars the outflow tract.
complications.presentation: VT with LBBB pattern, often in young athletes; RVOT dilatation on echo or CMR.
complications.hook: LBBB-pattern VT in a young athlete

student.hook: Read a PVC by its shape
student.text: LBBB-like means it starts in the RV (the LV activates late); an inferior axis means it starts high and travels down. Together: RVOT.
In tetralogy of Fallot, how narrow the RVOT is decides how blue the child is.

resident.text: Frequent RVOT PVCs in a normal heart are usually benign. A high burden on Holter (about 10% or more of beats) can weaken the LV (PVC cardiomyopathy): treat with a beta-blocker, a non-dihydropyridine CCB or ablation.
T inversion beyond V1–V3 in an adult, epsilon wave, a dilated RV, family history of sudden death. Think ARVC.

saq.q: A PVC has an LBBB shape with an inferior axis. Where does it probably start, and how do you know?
saq.a: In the RVOT: an LBBB shape means it starts in the RV (the LV activates late), and an inferior axis means it starts high and travels down.

saq.q: Name two findings that make 'RVOT ectopy' not benign and suggest ARVC.
saq.a: Any two: T inversion beyond V1–V3 in an adult, an epsilon wave, a dilated or poorly moving RV, a family history of sudden death, polymorphic or exercise VT with syncope.

cards.name: Interatrial septum
cards.core: The wall between the atria; most of the true septum is the thin fossa ovalis and its muscular rim.

quick.text: True septum = **fossa ovalis floor + limbus**
ASD: **fixed, wide split S2** + pulmonary flow murmur
Secundum ASD: **right axis + rSR′**; primum: **left axis**
Judge it in **subcostal**; A4C shows false dropout

anatomy.summary: An oblique wall whose true septal part is small: the fossa floor and its rim.
anatomy.detail: An oblique wall facing forwards and to the right. The true septum is small: the floor of the fossa ovalis (from the septum primum) and its rim (limbus); much of what looks like septum is folded atrial wall. In front and above it lies the aortic root; behind and below, the IVC and coronary sinus openings.

function.summary: Separates the atria; before birth the foramen ovale passed IVC blood to the LA.
function.detail: Keeps the two atrial circulations apart. Before birth, the foramen ovale lets oxygen-rich IVC blood cross from the RA to the LA; after birth, LA pressure rises above RA pressure and closes the flap.

supply.summary: RCA and LCx atrial branches.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the RCA and LCx.

relations.why: A transseptal puncture placed too far forward can enter the aorta.
Sinus venosus defects sit at this junction, often with an anomalous right upper pulmonary vein.
The fast pathway enters from the septum.

echo.text: Best TTE view: the beam crosses the septum at a right angle.
The thin fossa often drops out (false 'hole').
Between the atria at the level of the aortic valve.

cut.text: From the RA side, with the fossa ovalis.
From the LA side.

ecg.text: Secundum ASD: right axis with rSR′ in V1. Primum ASD: left axis with rSR′.

complications.name: Atrial septal defects
complications.mechanism: Secundum (in the fossa floor, commonest), primum (lower septum, part of an AV septal defect, often with a cleft mitral valve), sinus venosus (near the SVC), coronary sinus (unroofed). Blood shunts left to right and overloads the right heart.
complications.presentation: Often silent until adulthood; breathlessness, atrial arrhythmias, fixed wide split S2, pulmonary flow murmur.
complications.hook: Fixed split S2, right-heart volume load

complications.name: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the septum
complications.mechanism: Fat thickens the septum but spares the fossa ovalis (dumbbell shape).
complications.presentation: Benign echo finding that can be mistaken for a mass; sometimes atrial arrhythmias.

student.hook: Fixed, wide split S2 in ASD
student.text: The right heart carries extra volume, so the pulmonary valve closes late, and breathing changes both atria together.
The ASD itself is silent (little pressure difference between the atria). The murmur comes from extra flow across the pulmonary valve.
The septum primum grows down, a hole opens in it (ostium secundum), the septum secundum overlaps it, and the gap between them is the foramen ovale.

resident.text: Judge the septum in the subcostal view; the apical 4-chamber view shows false dropout. A bubble (agitated saline) study shows shunting.
Close an ASD when the right heart is volume-loaded and pulmonary vascular resistance is not severely raised; secundum defects with adequate rims can be closed with a device.

saq.q: Explain the fixed, wide split S2 in an ASD.
saq.a: The right heart carries extra volume, so the RV empties later and P2 is late (wide split). Breathing changes both atria together through the defect, so the split does not change (fixed).

saq.q: Which TTE view is best for the interatrial septum, and why can the apical 4-chamber view mislead?
saq.a: The subcostal view: the beam crosses the septum at a right angle. In A4C the beam runs parallel to the thin fossa, which drops out and mimics a defect.

sources: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guideline
ASE 2015 guidelines on echo for ASD/PFO

cards.name: Fossa ovalis
cards.core: The thin oval floor of the atrial septum, left by the fetal foramen ovale: the site of a PFO, a secundum ASD and transseptal puncture.

quick.text: Oval hollow in the septum, ringed by the **limbus**
**PFO** = flap (shunts only when RA > LA); **ASD** = hole (always shunts)
**Paradoxical embolism**: leg clot → PFO → stroke
**Bubble study + Valsalva** shows a PFO

anatomy.summary: Thin floor from the septum primum flap, ringed by the limbus.
anatomy.detail: A shallow oval hollow on the RA side of the septum, ringed in front and above by the muscular limbus. Its floor is the old septum primum flap; from the LA side its edge is a faint crescent. The Eustachian valve at the IVC opening points towards it.

function.summary: Fetal one-way valve that seals after birth when LA pressure rises.
function.detail: Before birth it was a one-way valve: the Eustachian valve steered oxygen-rich IVC blood through it into the LA and on to the brain. After birth, higher LA pressure presses the flap against the limbus; in most people they fuse.

supply.summary: No separate supply of clinical importance.
supply.detail: No clinically important separate supply (atrial septal branches).

relations.why: Venous blood from the IVC streams towards it, which is how a venous clot can reach a PFO.
Lies in front and above: the landmark to stay away from during transseptal puncture.

echo.text: The thin floor of the septum.
Often drops out; do not call an ASD from this view alone.

cut.text: Oval hollow ringed by the limbus.
Crescent edge of the flap from the LA side.

complications.name: Patent foramen ovale and paradoxical embolism
complications.mechanism: The flap never fused (about a quarter of adults); it opens when RA pressure rises above LA pressure (cough, strain, PE), letting a venous clot cross.
complications.presentation: Cryptogenic stroke in a younger patient; also decompression illness in divers and platypnoea–orthodeoxia.
complications.hook: Cryptogenic stroke in a younger patient

complications.name: Secundum ASD
complications.mechanism: The floor is deficient, leaving a true hole.
complications.presentation: Left-to-right shunt with right-heart volume overload.

complications.name: Atrial septal aneurysm
complications.mechanism: A floppy, redundant floor that swings between the atria.
complications.presentation: Often with a PFO; raises the stroke risk linked to a PFO.
complications.hook: Floppy septum, often with a PFO

student.text: A PFO is a flap that opens only when RA pressure beats LA pressure (no shunt at rest); an ASD is a hole that shunts left to right all the time.
A clot from a leg vein can cause a stroke only if it crosses to the left heart: paradoxical embolism through a PFO.

resident.hook: Cryptogenic stroke in a younger patient
resident.text: Bubble study with Valsalva. PFO closure helps selected patients under about 60 with a high-risk PFO (large shunt or septal aneurysm).
The RoPE score estimates how likely a PFO is the cause of a stroke rather than a bystander.

fellow.text: The transseptal puncture site is chosen for the procedure: lower and more posterior for pulmonary vein isolation and mitral edge-to-edge repair, adapted for LAA occlusion.

saq.q: What is the difference between a PFO and a secundum ASD?
saq.a: A PFO is an unsealed flap that opens only when RA pressure exceeds LA pressure, so there is no shunt at rest. A secundum ASD is a true hole in the fossa floor that shunts left to right all the time.
keys: PFO = flap, opens only when RA > LA

saq.q: A 45-year-old with cryptogenic stroke has a large PFO with an atrial septal aneurysm. What do you discuss?
saq.a: This is a high-risk PFO in a patient under 60: after other causes are excluded, PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy lowers recurrence compared with antiplatelets alone. Decide with a heart–brain team.

cards.name: Interventricular septum
cards.core: The wall between the ventricles: it works as part of the LV and carries the His bundle and both bundle branches.

quick.text: Muscular wall with a small **membranous** top under the aortic cusps
Carries the **His bundle, LBB and RBB**; fires first, left → right
Septal **q in I, V6** and **r in V1**; lost in LBBB
**D-shaped LV** = RV overload (systolic: pressure; diastolic: volume)
Post-MI **septal rupture**: new harsh murmur + shock

anatomy.summary: Thick muscle with a small membranous part; His on the crest, a bundle branch on each face.
anatomy.detail: Mostly thick muscle; a small membranous part at the top lies under the right and non-coronary aortic cusps. It bulges into the RV, so the LV is round in short axis. The His bundle runs on its crest under the membranous part; the left bundle fans down its LV side and the right bundle runs down its RV side to the moderator band. In older people the basal septum often bulges into the LVOT (sigmoid septum).

function.summary: Works with the LV; its shape shows the LV–RV pressure balance.
function.detail: Thickens towards the LV in systole. It depolarises first, from left to right. Its position shows the pressure balance between the ventricles: RV overload flattens it (D-shaped LV).

supply.summary: LAD perforators (front two thirds) and the PDA (back third).
supply.detail: Anterior two thirds from LAD septal perforators; posterior third from septal branches of the PDA.

relations.why: Septal infarction, surgery or septal reduction can block conduction.
Basal septal thickening narrows the outflow (HCM).

relations.with: Septal tricuspid leaflet and aortic cusps
relations.why: Perimembranous VSDs sit right next to them.

echo.text: Septal thickness (IVSd).
Shape: flattening = RV overload (D-sign).
Inferior septum and apex.

cut.text: Between the ventricles, with the His–bundle branches drawn.
Curved wall between round LV and crescent RV.
RV face with the moderator band.

ecg.text: Septal depolarisation: small q in I, aVL, V5–V6 and small r in V1. LBBB removes the septal q. Septal MI: V1–V2.

complications.name: Ventricular septal defect (congenital)
complications.mechanism: A hole, most often perimembranous, sometimes muscular; blood shunts left to right.
complications.presentation: Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; large defects cause heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.
complications.hook: Harsh holosystolic murmur, left lower sternal border

complications.name: Septal rupture after MI
complications.mechanism: Necrotic septum tears: apical after LAD occlusion, basal after inferior MI.
complications.presentation: A few days after MI: new harsh murmur, shock; oxygen step-up in the RV.

complications.name: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy (HCM)
complications.mechanism: Sarcomere mutation thickens the septum more than the other walls.
complications.presentation: Septum ≥ 15 mm, outflow obstruction, arrhythmia risk.

complications.name: Bundle branch block
complications.mechanism: Disease of the septum (ischaemia, fibrosis, procedures) damages the bundles that run on it.
complications.presentation: Wide QRS: LBBB or RBBB pattern.

student.text: The high LV–RV pressure difference drives a fast jet. A large VSD can be quiet and leads to pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger) if not closed.

student.hook: The septum fires first, left to right
student.text: That is the small q in I and V6 and the small r in V1. LBBB reverses it, so the septal q disappears.
A D-shaped LV in short axis means the RV is pushing on the septum.

resident.text: Flattening in systole means RV pressure overload (pulmonary hypertension, PE); flattening in diastole means RV volume overload (ASD, severe TR).
Maximal wall thickness ≥ 15 mm (≥ 13 mm with a family history) without another cause. Septal reduction (myectomy or alcohol ablation) is for symptomatic gradients ≥ 50 mmHg despite medicines.
After alcohol septal ablation expect RBBB; after surgical myectomy expect LBBB; both carry a risk of complete heart block.

saq.q: Why does a small VSD give a louder murmur than a large one?
saq.a: A small hole keeps a big LV–RV pressure difference, so the jet is fast and loud. A large hole lets the pressures equalise, so the jet is slow and quiet.
keys: Small hole keeps the pressure gap

saq.q: What makes the small q in I and V6, and why does LBBB remove it?
saq.a: The septum depolarises first, from left to right, which points away from the lateral leads (q in I, V6) and towards V1 (small r). In LBBB the septum is activated from the right, so the q disappears.
keys: q in I/V6, r in V1

saq.q: On PSAX the septum flattens only in diastole. What does this tell you?
saq.a: RV volume overload (e.g. ASD, severe TR). Flattening in systole would mean RV pressure overload.

sources: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guideline
verify: Rupture sites: apical after LAD, basal after inferior MI

cards.name: Tricuspid valve
cards.core: The RV inlet valve: three leaflets on a large, flexible ring that leaks easily when the RV or its ring dilates.

quick.text: Between **RA and RV**; its septal hinge sits a little **lower (more apical)** than the mitral
Three leaflets: **anterior** (largest), **posterior**, **septal**
Most TR is **functional**: the RV and ring dilate (pulmonary hypertension, AF)
TR murmur **louder on inspiration**; giant **v waves** in the JVP
**Injecting drug use** → tricuspid endocarditis, septic lung emboli

parts.name: Anterior leaflet
parts.note: The largest leaflet; most of its chordae come from the anterior papillary muscle, which the moderator band reaches.

parts.name: Posterior leaflet
parts.note: The smallest, along the inferior (diaphragmatic) wall of the RV.

parts.name: Septal leaflet
parts.note: Hinged on the septum a little lower than the mitral hinge; the His bundle runs just below its attachment, near the membranous septum.

anatomy.summary: Three leaflets on a large, flexible ring, held by the RV papillary muscles, including the anterior one reached by the moderator band.
anatomy.detail: The largest valve ring in the heart, between RA and RV. Anterior, posterior and septal leaflets take chordae from the anterior, posterior and small septal papillary muscles, and some straight from the septum. The septal hinge is normally a few millimetres closer to the apex than the mitral hinge. The ring has little fibrous support along the free wall, so it dilates mostly there.

function.summary: Opens in diastole at low pressure and closes at the start of systole (tricuspid part of S1).
function.detail: Flow across it rises with inspiration (more venous return), so right-sided murmurs get louder on inspiration. Whether it seals depends on the size and shape of the RV as much as on the leaflets.

supply.summary: The leaflets have no vessels of importance; the papillary muscles are fed by RCA and LAD branches.
supply.detail: Anterior papillary muscle: RCA and LAD (via the moderator-band artery). Posterior papillary muscle: RCA / PDA.

relations.why: Lie close to the septal hinge: tricuspid surgery and VSD closure can cause heart block.

relations.with: Right coronary artery in the right AV groove
relations.why: Runs around the ring and can be injured during annuloplasty.
Neighbours on the RA floor; the flutter isthmus runs from the IVC to this ring.

echo.text: Septal and lateral leaflets; the TR jet and its velocity give RV systolic pressure.
Beside the aortic valve, on the left of the image.
Leaflets and TR jet when apical views are poor.

cut.text: Opened RV: leaflets, chordae, papillary muscles.
Hinge slightly lower than the mitral.
From above, beside the mitral valve.

ecg.text: No direct sign; severe TR enlarges the RA (tall P waves) and often comes with AF.

complications.name: Functional tricuspid regurgitation
complications.mechanism: RV dilation (pulmonary hypertension, left-heart disease, AF) stretches the ring and pulls the leaflets apart.
complications.presentation: Raised JVP with giant v waves, pulsatile liver, oedema, ascites; holosystolic murmur louder on inspiration.
complications.hook: Raised JVP, v waves, louder on inspiration

complications.name: Tricuspid endocarditis
complications.mechanism: Bacteria from injected drugs or long-term lines settle on the leaflets (often S. aureus).
complications.presentation: Fever, septic pulmonary emboli (several cavitating lung nodules), new TR.
complications.hook: Injecting drugs, fever, septic lung emboli

complications.name: Ebstein anomaly
complications.mechanism: The septal and posterior leaflets are hinged far down in the RV, turning part of the RV into atrium.
complications.presentation: Cyanosis or heart failure, severe TR, often an accessory pathway (WPW).

complications.name: Carcinoid heart disease
complications.mechanism: Serotonin from liver metastases thickens and stiffens right-sided valves; the lung inactivates it before it reaches the left heart.
complications.presentation: TR (and pulmonary stenosis) with flushing and diarrhoea.

complications.name: Lead-related TR
complications.mechanism: A pacemaker or ICD lead crossing the valve holds a leaflet open.
complications.presentation: New or worse TR after a device.
complications.hook: TR that starts after a device

student.hook: Why right-sided murmurs grow on inspiration
student.text: Inspiration lowers chest pressure, more blood returns to the right heart, and more flows across the tricuspid valve (Carvallo sign).
On the 4-chamber view the tricuspid hinge is a little closer to the apex than the mitral: a quick way to tell the RV from the LV. Far lower suggests Ebstein anomaly.
The lung breaks down serotonin, so carcinoid plaques hit the tricuspid and pulmonary valves unless there is a shunt or lung metastases.

resident.hook: The TR jet gives RV pressure
resident.text: RV systolic pressure ≈ 4 × (peak TR velocity)² + RA pressure; a TR velocity above 2.8 m/s suggests pulmonary hypertension.

resident.hook: Check the TV during left-sided surgery
resident.text: Repair the tricuspid valve at mitral surgery when TR is severe, or moderate with a dilated ring.
Several cavitating lung nodules in a febrile person who injects drugs: blood cultures and an echo for tricuspid vegetations.

fellow.text: Edge-to-edge repair or transcatheter replacement is an option for severe symptomatic TR at high surgical risk.

saq.q: A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border gets louder on inspiration. Which valve, and why?
saq.a: Tricuspid regurgitation: inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so more blood leaks back through the tricuspid valve.

saq.q: Why does carcinoid heart disease usually spare the left-sided valves?
saq.a: Serotonin from liver metastases reaches the right heart first and is broken down in the lung, so it rarely reaches the left heart unless there is a shunt or lung metastases.

saq.q: Peak TR velocity 3.5 m/s, RA pressure about 10 mmHg. Estimate RV systolic pressure.
saq.a: 4 × 3.5² + 10 ≈ 59 mmHg: raised, suggesting pulmonary hypertension if there is no pulmonary stenosis.

verify: Papillary muscle supply of the TV
Ring dilation threshold for concomitant repair (≥ 40 mm or > 21 mm/m²)

cards.name: Aortic valve
cards.core: The LV outlet valve: three semilunar cusps whose sinuses give rise to the coronary arteries.

quick.text: At the root of the aorta, between the **mitral valve** and the **RVOT**, at the centre of the heart
Cusps are named by their **coronary**: right, left and non-coronary
**Severe AS + symptoms** (angina, syncope, breathlessness) = replace the valve
AS: **ejection murmur to the carotids**, slow pulse; AR: **early diastolic** murmur, wide pulse pressure
Disease near the **non-coronary cusp** can block the **His bundle**

parts.name: Right coronary cusp
parts.note: The most anterior cusp; the right coronary artery arises from its sinus.

parts.name: Left coronary cusp
parts.note: The left main coronary artery arises from its sinus.

parts.name: Non-coronary cusp
parts.note: Posterior, facing the atrial septum. It sits above the membranous septum and His bundle, so root disease or surgery here can cause heart block.

anatomy.summary: Three semilunar cusps, each with a sinus of Valsalva behind it, at the centre of the heart; no chordae.
anatomy.detail: The cusps hang from a crown-shaped attachment. The right and left coronary arteries arise from two of the sinuses. Behind, the valve is joined to the anterior mitral leaflet (aorto-mitral curtain); in front lies the RVOT; below the right and non-coronary cusps lie the membranous septum and the His bundle.

function.summary: Opens passively in systole and closes in diastole (A2); with the valve closed, the coronaries fill.
function.detail: Normal area is 3–4 cm². Most coronary flow happens in diastole, so in severe AR the low diastolic pressure cuts coronary perfusion. A2 normally comes just before P2.

supply.summary: The cusps have no vessels; the coronary ostia sit in the sinuses just above them.
supply.detail: The ostia usually lie below the sinotubular junction. Bulky calcium or a transcatheter valve can cover an ostium (a TAVI risk).

relations.why: Calcium or a TAVI valve can block them.
Below the right and non-coronary cusps: heart block after surgery or TAVI, and in root abscesses.
Shares the aorto-mitral curtain: endocarditis spreads between the two valves.

echo.text: Cusp opening and calcium; LVOT and aortic root size.
Three cusps ('Mercedes' sign); a bicuspid valve opens as a fish-mouth.
Doppler: stenosis velocity and gradient, regurgitant jets.

cut.text: Centre of the base, wedged between the other three valves.
Above the LVOT.

ecg.text: Stenosis or regurgitation causes LVH voltages with strain; root disease can cause PR prolongation or heart block.

complications.name: Aortic stenosis
complications.mechanism: Calcific degeneration (older age) or a bicuspid valve (earlier) narrows the opening; the LV thickens to push through it.
complications.presentation: Exertional angina, syncope or breathlessness; ejection murmur to the carotids, slow-rising pulse, soft A2.

complications.name: Aortic regurgitation
complications.mechanism: Damaged cusps (endocarditis, rheumatic, bicuspid) or a dilated root (Marfan, aortitis) let blood fall back in diastole, volume-loading the LV.
complications.presentation: Wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses, early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge; acute AR causes sudden pulmonary oedema.
complications.hook: Wide pulse pressure, early diastolic murmur

complications.name: Bicuspid aortic valve
complications.mechanism: Two cusps instead of three; turbulent flow wears them early; often with a dilated aorta and coarctation.
complications.presentation: Stenosis or regurgitation decades earlier than usual; ejection click.
complications.hook: Early AS or AR, dilated aorta, coarctation

complications.name: Endocarditis with root abscess
complications.mechanism: Infection spreads into the ring next to the membranous septum and conduction axis.
complications.presentation: Fever and new AR; a new long PR or heart block points to an abscess.
complications.hook: New AV block in endocarditis = abscess

complications.name: Heart block or coronary occlusion after TAVI
complications.mechanism: The prosthesis presses on the conduction axis below the non- and right cusps, or pushes calcium over a coronary ostium.
complications.presentation: New LBBB or complete heart block; sudden hypotension with ST changes during the procedure.
complications.hook: New LBBB, heart block or ostial occlusion

student.text: Angina, syncope and breathlessness on exertion. Once symptoms start, survival without valve replacement falls quickly.

student.hook: Why AR widens the pulse pressure
student.text: A big stroke volume raises systolic pressure; blood falling back into the LV drops diastolic pressure.
About 1–2% of people have one; it calcifies decades earlier than a three-cusp valve and often comes with a dilated aorta.

resident.text: Peak velocity ≥ 4 m/s, mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, valve area ≤ 1.0 cm². Symptoms or LVEF < 50% → valve replacement.
Small area but low gradient with a low EF: dobutamine echo separates true severe AS from pseudo-severe; a CT calcium score helps when the EF is normal.
In severe AS, vasodilators and sudden falls in preload (spinal anaesthesia, dehydration) can drop blood pressure sharply.
Suspect an aortic root abscess: TOE and urgent surgical review.

fellow.text: A heart-team choice based on age, surgical risk, anatomy (bicuspid valve, coronary heights, annulus size) and life expectancy.

saq.q: Name the classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis and explain exertional syncope.
saq.a: Angina, syncope and breathlessness. On exertion the vessels dilate but the narrow valve cannot raise output, so blood pressure and brain perfusion fall.

saq.q: Why does aortic regurgitation produce a wide pulse pressure?
saq.a: The LV ejects a large stroke volume (high systolic pressure), and blood falls back into the LV in diastole (low diastolic pressure).

saq.q: Peak velocity 4.3 m/s, mean gradient 46 mmHg, area 0.8 cm², LVEF 60%, new breathlessness on stairs. Next step?
saq.a: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis: refer to the heart team for aortic valve replacement (surgical or TAVI).

cards.name: Pulmonary valve
cards.core: The RV outlet valve: three thin semilunar cusps at the top of the RVOT, working at low pressure.

quick.text: The **highest, most anterior** valve, at the top of the RVOT, left of the aortic valve
**P2** is loud in pulmonary hypertension and splits from A2 on inspiration
**Pulmonary stenosis** is usually congenital: tetralogy of Fallot, Noonan syndrome
Severe **pulmonary regurgitation** is common years after Fallot repair

parts.name: Cusps
parts.note: Three thin semilunar cusps (anterior, right, left); no coronary arteries arise from their sinuses.

anatomy.summary: Three thin cusps on the muscular RVOT; no fibrous link to the tricuspid valve.
anatomy.detail: Sits higher and more anterior than the aortic valve, on a free-standing muscular funnel (which is why it can be moved in the Ross operation). The two outflow tracts cross: the pulmonary trunk runs back and to the left of the aorta.

function.summary: Opens in systole and closes in diastole (P2), at about a fifth of systemic pressure.
